Perpetual
per-PECH-oo-ul
adj.
From Latin perpetuus, continuous, unbroken, from per (through) and petere (to go toward). Webster 1828: never ceasing; continuing forever in future time; unfailing. In the Authorized Version perpetual renders Hebrew words of unbroken continuance, and it is applied to statutes, to covenants, to the fire on the altar — and, once, with terrible irony, to backsliding.

Biblical Definition

Perpetual in Scripture describes what does not stop, and its most frequent home is the law of the sanctuary. The sabbath is kept throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant (Exodus 31:16). The dietary boundary is set as a perpetual statute for your generations throughout all your dwellings (Leviticus 3:17). The fire on the altar was never to go out. In each case the word does two things at once: it binds Israel across time, and it testifies that the God who commanded is Himself unchanging. Jeremiah then carries the term into the promise of the new covenant, where it becomes gospel rather than regulation: Come, and let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten (Jeremiah 50:5). The unbrokenness has moved from the observance to the LORD who keeps it, which is precisely the difference between the two covenants. And the same prophet turns the word against his people with devastating precision: Why then is this people of Jerusalem slidden back by a perpetual backsliding? (Jeremiah 8:5). Man is capable of perpetuity too. Left to himself he is unbroken in only one direction, and that verse names it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PERPETUAL as never ceasing; continuing forever in future time; destined to be eternal; unfailing; everlasting; also, continued without intermission, and permanent as opposed to temporary.

expand to see more

PERPETUAL, a. [L. perpetuus, from perpes, perpetis.] — Never ceasing; continuing forever in future time; destined to be eternal; as a perpetual covenant. Continuing without intermission; uninterrupted; as a perpetual stream. Permanent; fixed; not temporary.

Webster’s two senses — forever in future time and without intermission — are both needed. A perpetual statute binds every generation; a perpetual fire is never allowed to die on any single night. Israel had to obey the word in both directions at once, which is why the priesthood was staffed around the clock.

Key Scripture

Exodus 31:16 — "Wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant."

Leviticus 3:17 — "It shall be a perpetual statute for your generations throughout all your dwellings, that ye eat neither fat nor blood."

Jeremiah 50:5 — "They shall ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward, saying, Come, and let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten."

Jeremiah 8:5 — "Why then is this people of Jerusalem slidden back by a perpetual backsliding? they hold fast deceit, they refuse to return."

Leviticus 6:13 — "The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out."

Modern Corruption

Perpetual is corrupted when the perpetuity of Israel’s ceremonial statutes is used either to bind the church to abrogated ceremonies, or, in the opposite error, to argue that God’s promises expire because His ceremonies did.

expand to see more

Because the Authorized Version calls the ceremonial statutes perpetual, two contrary errors have grown from the word. The first insists that whatever God called perpetual must still bind, and so reinstates dietary law, the seventh-day sabbath as ceremony, or a standing sacrificial calendar. The Reformed answer distinguishes the moral, ceremonial, and judicial law: the moral law abides because it reflects God’s character; the ceremonial was perpetual for the age it governed and is fulfilled and therefore ended in Christ, which is Hebrews’ entire argument. A shadow is not abolished when the body arrives — it is answered. The fire on the altar was to burn without going out, and it does not burn now, because the offering it served has been made once for all.

The second error runs the other way and is more damaging. Observing that God’s perpetual ceremonies did in fact cease, it concludes that His covenant language is loose, and that promises to His people may likewise lapse. Jeremiah forecloses this. The perpetual covenant he announces is one that shall not be forgotten, and its unbrokenness rests on the LORD rather than on Israel’s observance — which is exactly why it holds where the first covenant did not. God’s faithfulness is the constant; the administration changes. And Jeremiah 8:5 supplies the sober counterweight, because perpetual backsliding is a real human capacity. Unbroken continuance is not automatically a virtue. Everything depends on the direction of the line.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Two Hebrew words carry perpetual. One means the age-long stretch of time; the other means continual, regular, without a gap. The first governs covenants, the second governs the daily service — and the difference explains why some perpetual things ceased and others did not.

expand to see more

Hebrew ōlām (H5769) — long duration, antiquity, futurity; the age-long word rendered perpetual, everlasting, and for ever (Exodus 31:16; Leviticus 3:17).

Hebrew tāmīd (H8548) — continual, regular, uninterrupted; the word behind the daily burnt offering and the fire that never went out (Leviticus 6:13).

The word ōlām measures the span of an age and takes its length from the thing it modifies; applied to God it is absolute, applied to a ceremony it runs to that ceremony’s fulfilment.

Hebrew āvōn (H5771) — iniquity, guilt; the condition Jeremiah 8:5 diagnoses as perpetual backsliding, where man’s own continuance runs the wrong way.

Usage

"A perpetual statute for your generations (Leviticus 3:17) binds an age, not every age — the shadow ends when the body comes."

"Jeremiah’s perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten (Jeremiah 50:5) rests its unbrokenness on the LORD, not on the observer."

"A perpetual backsliding (Jeremiah 8:5): man is capable of unbroken continuance too, and by nature only in one direction."
